sources.locator: CS2023 Software Development Fundamentals; August 2023; section applicable to Hardware and software roles
sources.claim: A processor executes instructions, working memory holds active instructions and data, storage retains files, devices exchange data, and the operating system coordinates access to hardware.

canonicalExplanation.summary: Your computer is a team. The **processor (CPU)** does the work, **memory (RAM)** holds what it's working on *right now*, **storage** keeps files when the power is off, **devices** move data in and out, and the **operating system** is the manager who decides who gets what.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
Ever had your laptop slow to a crawl with 40 browser tabs open — even though your disk had tons of free space? That's not a mystery once you know who does what inside a computer. By the end of this lesson you'll be able to point at any everyday action — opening a photo, playing a song — and say which part of the machine is doing the work.

```predict
{"question": "Your disk has 500 GB free, but the laptop is slow with 40 tabs open. What's most likely full?", "options": ["Storage (the disk)", "Working memory (RAM)", "The screen"], "answer": 1, "why": "Open tabs live in **working memory (RAM)**, which is much smaller than storage. Free disk space doesn't help once RAM is full."}
```

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.body: You should already know **Program, code and algorithm** — the difference between a method, its written code, and a runnable program. Here we look at the machine that actually runs that program.

sections.heading: The mental model: a kitchen crew
sections.body:
| Part | Kitchen job | What it really does |
|---|---|---|
| Processor (CPU) | The chef | Executes instructions, one tiny step after another, very fast. |
| Working memory (RAM) | The countertop | Holds the data and instructions in use *now*; wiped when power goes off. |
| Storage (SSD/disk) | The pantry | Keeps files permanently, but slower to reach. |
| Devices | Doors & windows | Keyboard, screen, network, speakers — data in and out. |
| Operating system | The head waiter | Decides which program gets the chef, the counter and the doors. |

```reveal
{"prompt": "You close a document without saving and the power cuts out. Why is your latest change gone?", "answer": "Unsaved changes live only in **working memory**, which is cleared when power is lost. Saving copies them to **storage**, which keeps data without power."}
```

sections.heading: Who does what when you open a file
sections.body:
When you double-click `holiday.jpg`:

1. The **operating system** finds the file in **storage** and starts the image app.
2. The file's bytes are copied into **working memory**.
3. The **processor** decodes those bytes into pixels.
4. The **display** (a device) shows them.

```predict
{"question": "Which step would get faster if you bought a bigger (but equally fast) disk?", "options": ["None of them, really", "Decoding the pixels", "Showing the image"], "answer": 0, "why": "A *bigger* disk stores more, but it doesn't read faster or give the processor more working memory. More space ≠ more speed."}
```

includes: Name the role of processor, working memory, storage, devices and operating system.
Explain which part limits a given everyday slowdown.
excludes: How transistors and caches work internally.

outcomes: Explain where instructions and data reside while a small program runs.

examples.title: Cropping a photo
examples.situation: You open `holiday.jpg` in an image editor, crop it, and see the smaller photo on screen.
walkthrough: **Storage → working memory:** the operating system reads the compressed file bytes from the disk and loads them into RAM.
**Processor:** the CPU runs the editor's crop instructions, changing the pixel data held in working memory.
**Device:** the display shows the updated pixels. Nothing is saved to storage until you press Save.
examples.result: The cropped photo appears on screen; the file in storage is unchanged until you save.

examples.title: The slow laptop with a huge disk
examples.situation: A laptop has 1 TB of free disk space but only 8 GB of RAM, and freezes with a big game plus 40 tabs open.
walkthrough: List what's running: the game and every tab need space in working memory.
Compare sizes: 8 GB of RAM fills up long before 1 TB of storage matters.
When RAM is full the OS shuffles data to storage ("swapping"), which is far slower — that's the freeze.
examples.result: Closing tabs frees RAM and the laptop speeds up; more free disk space would not have helped.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: Adding more disk storage always makes every running program faster, because storage and working memory are the same thing.
misconceptions.correction: Storage keeps files long-term; working memory holds what running programs use right now. They're different resources, so extra storage space doesn't speed up programs that are short on working memory.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In "The slow laptop with a huge disk", which resource is actually full?

analogy.example: A restaurant kitchen: the **chef** is the processor, the **countertop** is working memory, the **pantry** is storage, the **doors** are devices, and the **head waiter** (operating system) decides whose order the chef cooks next.
usefulFor: remembering that counter space (RAM) is small and fast while the pantry (storage) is big and slow
seeing why a full counter slows everything down
limitations: A real CPU does billions of tiny steps per second and can juggle many programs by switching quickly — no chef can.
Modern chips have several cores, like several chefs sharing one counter.

steps.explanation: The operating system copies the file from storage into working memory so the app can use it.
The processor changes the pixel data sitting in working memory; storage is untouched.
The display device shows the new pixels. The file only changes if you save.

trace.textAlternative: Opening and cropping a photo. Step 1, Load: storage is holiday.jpg (compressed bytes); working memory is copy of those bytes. The operating system copies the file from storage into working memory so the app can use it. Step 2, Crop: processor is running crop instructions; working memory is pixels now 800x600. The processor changes the pixel data sitting in working memory; storage is untouched. Step 3, Show: display is cropped image; storage is still the original file. The display device shows the new pixels. The file only changes if you save.

faded.prompt: Walk through "Cropping a photo" in three lines: where the photo's bytes start, which part changes them, and where you see the result.
scaffold: Line 2: which part runs the crop instructions?
Line 3: which device shows it — and is the file saved yet?
expectedEvidence: Names the example "Cropping a photo": opening holiday.jpg in an image editor to crop it.
The operating system loads the file bytes from storage into working memory.
The processor runs the crop instructions on the pixels in working memory.
The display shows the cropped photo on screen; the file in storage is unchanged until you save.

nearTransfer.prompt: You stream a song: it arrives over Wi-Fi and plays through headphones. Name the part that handles each of: receiving the data, holding it briefly, decoding it, and playing it.
scaffold: Wi-Fi and headphones are both devices.
Where does data wait while being decoded?
expectedEvidence: Network device receives data; working memory buffers it; the processor decodes it; the headphones (device) play it.
Storage may not be involved at all when streaming.

farTransfer.prompt: Pick something you do daily on your phone. Explain which parts (processor, working memory, storage, devices, operating system) are involved and which one would most likely cause a slowdown.
scaffold: Don't reuse the kitchen analogy — name the real parts.
expectedEvidence: Correctly assigns roles to at least four parts.
Identifies a plausible bottleneck with a reason.

remediation.explanation: Open your system's task manager (Ctrl+Shift+Esc on Windows). Look at **Memory** vs **Disk**: memory is what running apps use now, disk is storage space. Open a few more tabs and watch memory climb while free disk space barely moves.
remediation.retryPrompt: Now explain again why the laptop in "The slow laptop with a huge disk" froze, using the words working memory and storage.

recap.summary: Processor = does the work. Working memory = what's in use right now (fast, small, wiped at power-off). Storage = files kept long-term (big, slower). Devices = data in and out. Operating system = coordinates it all. More storage space doesn't make programs faster when working memory is the bottleneck.
